"Below are questions proposed for a research problem, each with the reframing behind it. Classify each one.
kind: \"reframe\" if it changes what is computed, measured or ordered so that more compute buys something it did not before; \"copies\" if it only runs the same computation more times, on more items, or side by side; \"other\" otherwise.
meets_criterion: \"yes\" or \"no\" for this criterion: The question removes the closed-loop dependency: it scores steering effects on fixed, recorded observations (open loop) instead of full closed-loop episodes, and confirms only the top candidates with closed-loop episodes.
Give for each a quote from the proposal and a reason of at most 25 words. Decide only from the text below; do not use tools.
Problem:
Inference-time steering of VLA internals (SAEs, FFN vectors, conceptors, linear observers)
Steering a VLA's internal features can bring out behaviour the model already has, without retraining. On real DROID hardware, SAE steering of pi0.5 raised target-object grasps by +9 to +21 out of 25 trials, and ablating the top-4 general features cut success from 39/40 to 0/40. COAST conceptors raised pi0.5 on LIBERO-10 from 0.43 to 0.80, with about +40% on three real tasks. Grant et al. found motor programs bound to absolute coordinates (50/50 grasps at the recorded spot on a UR10e). All tests are rigid tabletop tasks; none is cloth or a dish rack. Goodfire markets steering for robotics but publishes no numbers.
What more compute would buy: The quantity is closed-loop rollouts and SAEs swept; the largest is 420,000+ rollouts and 520+ SAEs across six VLAs (https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.19233), and above that it is unknown whether any feature controls contact-rich or deformable behaviour, because every sweep so far ran rigid pick-and-place or drawer tasks.
What runs step after step: Each feature waits on an SAE fit (about 6,700 Adam steps, derived from https://arxiv.org/html/2603.19183; 'a few GPU-hours per SAE on one A100') and then on closed-loop rollouts of up to 300 steps, each waiting on a ~150 ms VLA forward pass and the next observation; the answer needed 150 rollouts × 135 features (20,250 episodes), and one unbatched rollout leaves the GPU idle while the simulator steps. Steps within a rollout must run in order, but rollouts are independent: batching hundreds of steered environments in a GPU-parallel simulator, with a separate hook per environment and simulation pipelined against inference, would run them together; this pays only if steering effects in simulation match the real robot (false for cloth). The nearest attempt is RLinf-VLA, 1.61-1.88x with 256 ManiSkill environments, for RL rather than interpretability (https://arxiv.org/html/2510.06710v2).
Proposals: [{\"index\":1,\"bottleneck\":\"Per-feature cost is set by binary-success statistics: ~150 closed-loop rollouts x 300 serial steps to detect a +9/25 effect, so the 20,250-episode sweep mostly narrows error bars on rigid pick-and-place; beyond batching (RLinf-VLA's 1.61-1.88x), more GPUs buy more of the same number.\",\"assumption\":\"That the answer to 'does this feature matter' must be an end-of-episode binary success rate, so one rollout yields one sample.\",\"reframe\":\"Change what is measured: log per-step continuous proxies inside rollouts that already run (contact impulse, slip events, goal-distance slope, cloth-coverage delta), turning one episode into hundreds of correlated samples and shifting compute from episodes-per-feature to features-and-tasks covered, including deformable sims.\",\"question\":\"Across ~10 known-effective and ~10 null features on rigid sim tasks, at what rollout count n does the Spearman correlation between proxy-estimated feature effects and the full 150-rollout success effects exceed 0.9?\",\"measure\":\"Steer 20 features x 150 rollouts x 300 steps in a ManiSkill-class GPU sim, logging proxies every step; bootstrap Spearman(proxy@n, success@150) vs n. About 3,000 batched sim rollouts, ~1-2 A100-days.\",\"compute_after\":\"If proxies rank-stabilize at n~10-30, the same budget screens 5-15x more features and tasks per GPU-hour, freeing budget for cloth/deformable sweeps instead of tighter CIs on rigid success.\",\"exact\":\"Proxy = per-step contact-impulse integral plus goal-distance slope; report Spearman rho vs n with 95% bootstrap CI; decision rule: rho>0.9 sustained for 10 consecutive values of n; features drawn from the published sweep so ground-truth effects exist.\",\"expected\":\"Proxies stabilize at n=10-30 because 300 steps per episode multiply effective samples and the known rigid-task effects (+9 to +21 of 25) are large.\",\"fails_if\":\"Proxy ranking at small n disagrees with success ranking for features whose benefit is long-horizon (recovery after slip, multi-stage tasks) and rho plateaus below ~0.8; then full episodes are the irreducible unit and the reframe buys nothing.\",\"closest_prior\":\"RLinf-VLA batched ManiSkill rollouts (arXiv:2510.06710) as harness; arXiv:2603.19233 (420k rollouts, 520 SAEs) as reference effects; off-policy-evaluation/variance-reduction literature as method.\"},{\"index\":2,\"bottleneck\":\"The serial unit is the 300-step closed-loop rollout (~150 ms VLA pass per step, GPU idle while the simulator steps); steps cannot be parallelized, and if contact dynamics amplify small errors, parallel-in-time evaluation is ruled out, capping wall-clock per feature regardless of GPU count.\",\"assumption\":\"That each evaluation must be an independent full-horizon episode starting from the initial state, so 150 rollouts means 150 x 300 serial steps.\",\"reframe\":\"Change the unit of work: run a few long unsteered rollouts with state checkpoints, then branch steered vs unsteered copies from each checkpoint for short horizons; all branches are independent and batch massively, and perturbed unsteered pairs from the same checkpoints directly measure the system's forgetfulness, deciding whether parallel-in-time rollout is even legal.\",\"question\":\"Do steered and unsteered branches from identical checkpointed states converge or drift apart with horizon h, and does the per-feature effect measured at h in {10,25,50} rank-match the full 300-step effect?\",\"measure\":\"In rigid sim: 20 base rollouts, checkpoint every 25 steps (~240 states), branch steered/unsteered pairs plus 1e-3-perturbed unsteered pairs for each h; ~2x10^4 short segments, ~1 A100-day batched.\",\"compute_after\":\"If effects are fixed by h<=50 and perturbations decay, evaluation becomes fully parallel short segments and parareal-style speculative rollout becomes viable, turning weeks of serial sweep wall-clock into hours and making cloth-sim sweeps cheap enough to attempt.\",\"exact\":\"Per feature: Delta(h) = mean(proxy_steered(h) - proxy_unsteered(h)) over shared checkpoints; report (a) Spearman(Delta(h), Delta(300)) vs h and (b) median state divergence of 1e-3-perturbed unsteered pairs vs h; 'forgetful' = divergence decays or saturates below the decision-relevant effect size.\",\"expected\":\"Rigid tabletop manipulation is damping-dominated between contacts; divergence saturates after each contact event and Delta(h) ranks match Delta(300) by h~25-50, giving 6-12x horizon shortening on top of batch parallelism.\",\"fails_if\":\"Perturbed pairs diverge through stick-slip contact sequences (near-chaotic) and Spearman stays <0.7 up to h=300; then serial closed-loop rollouts are irreducible, parallel-in-time is dead for this system, and only cross-rollout batching remains.\",\"closest_prior\":\"Parareal/parallel-in-time integration with its converge-or-drift-apart pre-test; RLinf-VLA batched environments (arXiv:2510.06710); tree-search/MPC branching used in manipulation planning.\"},{\"index\":3,\"bottleneck\":\"The pipeline fits then searches causally (~6,700 Adam steps per SAE, then 150 rollouts per feature), so almost all compute validates features that turn out null; and because every sweep ran rigid tasks, it is unknown whether any feature governs contact-rich or deformable behavior, so scaling the same sweep above 520 SAEs buys the same null result on the wrong tasks.\",\"assumption\":\"That candidates must be generated bottom-up (fit SAE, then causally sweep each feature) and that the search tasks are rigid tabletop ones.\",\"reframe\":\"Invert the order and retarget the objective: mine the already-collected 420k rollout logs (plus any recorded cloth episodes) for features whose activations separate success from failure or track contact events, spend rollouts only on verifying top correlational candidates, and aim verification at cloth/dish-rack contact metrics instead of rigid success.\",\"question\":\"Measured against the published sweep's known causal effects, what is precision@20 of ranking features by success-minus-failure activation gap, and does a candidate found this way on a deformable sim task move a cloth metric when clamped?\",\"measure\":\"Pure reanalysis: load stored activations/outcomes (or refit ~2 SAEs), rank all features by activation gap, compare to the sweep's causal ranking; a few A100-hours, zero new rollouts. Then one cloth-sim check: clamp top-5 features, 25 rollouts each, <1 GPU-day.\",\"compute_after\":\"If precision@20 is high, causal-validation rollouts per confirmed feature drop ~100x, and the freed budget moves to deformable tasks and to a handful of real-robot verifications rather than exhaustive rigid sweeps; compute then changes the answer (which features control cloth) instead of reproducing the rigid one.\",\"exact\":\"Gap = mean activation in success minus failure episodes (or correlation with per-step contact events); report precision@k and Kendall tau vs the sweep's causal ranking for k in {5,20,100}; cloth check: coverage delta vs unsteered baseline over 25 rollouts per feature, pre-registered effect threshold.\",\"expected\":\"The ablation result (top-4 general features cutting 39/40 to 0/40) implies a few features carry large effects, so correlational screening should recover them well above chance; COAST's data-fitted conceptors (0.43 to 0.80 on LIBERO-10) show data-first steering can work.\",\"fails_if\":\"Causal effects are thin and confounded (precision@20 near base rate), or sim-cloth candidates fail on real cloth, the sim-to-real ceiling no sim compute fixes; then the only remaining buy is real-robot rollouts, which do not batch, and the honest answer is that compute is not the blocker for cloth.\",\"closest_prior\":\"arXiv:2603.19233 (420k rollouts, 520 SAEs) as data and ground truth; COAST conceptors (arXiv:2603.19183 lineage) as data-driven steering; Grant et al. coordinate-bound motor programs (50/50 on UR10e) as evidence features can be read off data; Goodfire's number-free robotics marketing as the null baseline.\"}]

Return only one JSON value, with no other text, that matches this JSON Schema:
{\"type\":\"object\",\"required\":[\"items\"],\"properties\":{\"items\":{\"type\":\"array\",\"items\":{\"type\":\"object\",\"required\":[\"index\",\"kind\",\"meets_criterion\",\"quote\",\"reason\"],\"properties\":{\"index\":{\"type\":\"integer\"},\"kind\":{\"type\":\"string\",\"enum\":[\"reframe\",\"copies\",\"other\"]},\"meets_criterion\":{\"type\":\"string\",\"enum\":[\"yes\",\"no\",\"NA\"]},\"quote\":{\"type\":\"string\"},\"reason\":{\"type\":\"string\"}}}}}}"

Let me analyze each proposal carefully.

The problem: Inference-time steering of VLA internals. The key bottleneck context: closed-loop rollouts are serial (300 steps each), SAE fitting, then closed-loop rollouts per feature.

The criterion: "The question removes the closed-loop dependency: it scores steering effects on fixed, recorded observations (open loop) instead of full closed-loop episodes, and confirms only the top candidates with closed-loop episodes."

So the criterion is about: scoring steering effects on fixed, recorded observations (open-loop, i.e., using recorded data/logs, not running the policy in the loop), with closed-loop episodes only for confirming top candidates.

Kind classification:
- "reframe" if it changes what is computed, measured or ordered so that more compute buys something it did not before
- "copies" if it only runs the same computation more times, on more items, or side by side
- "other" otherwise

Proposal 1:
- Bottleneck: per-feature cost set by binary-success statistics, ~150 closed-loop rollouts.
- Reframe: change what is measured — log per-step continuous proxies inside rollouts that already run (contact impulse, slip events, goal-distance slope, cloth-coverage delta), turning one episode into hundreds of correlated samples. This changes what is measured — instead of end-of-episode binary success, measure per-step proxies. This is a reframe (changes what is measured so more compute buys more features/tasks coverage).
- Question: "Across ~10 known-effective and ~10 null features on rigid sim tasks, at what rollout count n does the Spearman correlation between proxy-estimated feature effects and the full 150-rollout success effects exceed 0.9?"
- Measure: steer 20 features × 150 rollouts × 300 steps in a GPU sim, logging proxies every step.
- Does it meet the criterion? The criterion: "scores steering effects on fixed, recorded observations (open loop) instead of full closed-loop episodes, and confirms only the top candidates with closed-loop episodes."
  - Proposal 1 still runs full closed-loop rollouts (steer 20 features × 150 rollouts × 300 steps); it just logs proxies within them. It does not score on fixed, recorded observations; it runs closed-loop episodes with proxies measured inside. So it does NOT meet the criterion. It's not open-loop on recorded observations; it's still closed-loop but with richer per-step measurements.
  - So meets_criterion: "no".
- Kind: reframe. It changes what is measured (per-step continuous proxies instead of binary end-of-episode success), so compute shifts from episodes-per-feature to features-and-tasks covered. Yes, reframe.
- Quote: something like "log per-step continuous proxies inside rollouts that already run (contact impulse, slip events, goal-distance slope, cloth-coverage delta), turning one episode into hundreds of correlated samples" — from the reframe field.
- Reason: Changes measured quantity from binary episode success to per-step proxies; but still runs full closed-loop rollouts, not open-loop scoring on recorded data.

Proposal 2:
- Bottleneck: serial 300-step closed-loop rollout.
- Reframe: change the unit of work: run a few long unsteered rollouts with state checkpoints, then branch steered vs unsteered copies from each checkpoint for short horizons; all branches independent and batch massively. Perturbed unsteered pairs measure forgetfulness, deciding whether parallel-in-time rollout is legal.
- Question: "Do steered and unsteered branches from identical checkpointed states converge or drift apart with horizon h, and does the per-feature effect measured at h in {10,25,50} rank-match the full 300-step effect?"
- Kind: reframe — changes what is computed (short branched segments from checkpoints instead of full episodes from initial state), enabling massive parallelism. This changes what is computed/measured so more compute buys something (wall-clock parallelism beyond cross-rollout batching). Yes, reframe.
- Meets criterion? Does it score steering effects on fixed, recorded observations (open loop)? The base rollouts are unsteered rollouts with checkpoints; then steered vs unsteered branches run from checkpoints — these are still closed-loop short-horizon episodes (the policy still acts and environment steps). It's not scoring on fixed recorded observations; it's short closed-loop segments from checkpointed states. It doesn't score on recorded observations in an open-loop fashion. It does short closed-loop segments. So it does not meet the criterion exactly. The criterion specifically requires open-loop scoring on fixed recorded observations. Proposal 2 uses short closed-loop branches, not open-loop scoring of recorded observations. So "no".
  - Hmm, but wait — could one argue that branching from checkpoints is like using recorded states? The criterion says "scores steering effects on fixed, recorded observations (open loop)". Open loop means: given recorded observations, apply the steered model to those observations and measure something (e.g., activation changes, predicted actions), without stepping the environment. Proposal 2 branches and runs the environment for h steps — that's closed-loop short horizon, not open-loop. So "no".
- Quote: "run a few long unsteered rollouts with state checkpoints, then branch steered vs unsteered copies from each checkpoint for short horizons; all branches are independent and batch massively"
- Reason: Changes unit of work from full serial episodes to parallel short branches; still closed-loop (short) segments, not open-loop scoring on recorded observations.

Proposal 3:
- Bottleneck: pipeline fits then searches causally; almost all compute validates null features; unknown whether features govern contact-rich/deformable behavior.
- Reframe: invert the order and retarget objective: mine already-collected 420k rollout logs for features whose activations separate success from failure or track contact events, spend rollouts only on verifying top correlational candidates, aim verification at cloth/dish-rack contact metrics.
- Question: "Measured against the published sweep's known causal effects, what is precision@20 of ranking features by success-minus-failure activation gap, and does a candidate found this way on a deformable sim task move a cloth metric when clamped?"
- Measure: pure reanalysis of stored activations/outcomes, rank features by activation gap, compare to causal ranking; then one cloth-sim check: clamp top-5 features, 25 rollouts each.
- Kind: reframe — changes what is computed and ordered (correlational mining of recorded logs first, causal rollouts only for top candidates; retargeting at cloth metrics). More compute buys new answers (which features control cloth) instead of reproducing rigid sweeps. Yes, reframe.
- Meets criterion? "scores steering effects on fixed, recorded observations (open loop) instead of full closed-loop episodes, and confirms only the top candidates with closed-loop episodes."
  - Proposal 3: mines already-collected rollout logs (fixed, recorded data) — scoring features by activation gap on recorded episodes. That's open-loop analysis on recorded observations (activations recorded in success/failure episodes). Then confirms only top candidates with closed-loop episodes (the cloth-sim check clamps top-5 features with 25 rollouts each).
  - This matches the criterion: it scores features on fixed, recorded observations (the stored 420k rollout logs, activations/outcomes), and confirms only top candidates with closed-loop episodes. Yes, meets criterion.
  - Is "steering effects" scored on recorded observations? The mining scores features by success-minus-failure activation gap on recorded logs — that's a correlational proxy for steering effect. The confirmation is closed-loop rollouts (cloth-sim clamping, 25 rollouts each; also possibly real-robot verifications). Yes, this is the open-loop screening + closed-loop confirmation pattern. So "yes".
- Quote: "mine the already-collected 420k rollout logs ... for features whose activations separate success from failure ..., spend rollouts only on verifying top correlational candidates"
- Reason: Scores candidate features on recorded rollout logs (open-loop), confirming only top candidates with closed-loop episodes; matches criterion.

Wait — the criterion says "it scores steering effects on fixed, recorded observations (open loop)". In proposal 3, the mining is of activations from recorded episodes — is that scoring "steering effects"? It ranks features by activation gap between success and failure episodes — a correlational proxy for steering effect. Then verification on top candidates. Hmm, one could argue the open-loop part doesn't directly measure "steering effects" (it doesn't apply steering to recorded observations and measure outcomes); it measures activation-outcome correlation. But the spirit of the criterion: remove closed-loop dependency by scoring on fixed recorded observations, confirming top candidates closed-loop. Proposal 3 does exactly that: the ranking is done purely on recorded data (zero new rollouts), and only top candidates get closed-loop verification (cloth-sim check). I'd say "yes".

Actually, let me reconsider. The criterion mentions "scores steering effects on fixed, recorded observations (open loop)". In proposal 3, does it apply steering to recorded observations? The measure says "Pure reanalysis: load stored activations/outcomes ... rank all features by activation gap". This is not applying steering; it's correlational mining. But then "does a candidate found this way on a deformable sim task move a cloth metric when clamped?" — clamping is steering, but that's in sim (closed-loop rollouts).

Hmm. The criterion has two parts: (1) scores steering effects on fixed recorded observations (open loop) instead of full closed-loop episodes; (2) confirms only top candidates with closed-loop episodes.

Proposal 3's primary scoring is on recorded observations — the ranking by activation gap on stored logs. That is open-loop in the sense that no new rollouts are needed for the ranking; it uses recorded data. Whether it's "steering effects" strictly — the activation gap between success and failure is a proxy for the causal steering effect, validated against the sweep's known causal ranking. The confirmation of top candidates happens with closed-loop episodes (the cloth-sim clamping check). I think this is the closest match to the criterion, so "yes".

Alternatively, one could be strict: the criterion says "scores steering effects... on fixed, recorded observations (open loop)". In proposal 3, the open-loop scoring doesn't involve applying steering to recorded observations and measuring the resulting behavior difference; it's correlational. But among the three proposals, proposal 3 is clearly the one designed to remove the closed-loop dependency by scoring on recorded logs and confirming only top candidates closed-loop. I'll say "yes".

Now let me also double-check proposal 1's kind. The reframe: "log per-step continuous proxies inside rollouts that already run ... shifting compute from episodes-per-feature to features-and-tasks covered". This changes what is measured — from binary success to per-step proxies — so more compute buys screening more features/tasks. That is a reframe. Yes.

Proposal 2's kind: changes the unit of work from full serial episodes to checkpoint-branching short segments, enabling parallelism and possibly parallel-in-time. This changes what is computed (short branched segments vs full episodes). More compute buys wall-clock reduction via parallelism beyond cross-rollout batching. Hmm — is this "reframe" or "copies"? The definition of "copies" is "it only runs the same computation more times, on more items, or side by side." Proposal 2's branching is running the same rollout computation... from checkpoints, in parallel. Actually, one could argue proposal 2 is about parallelism — running things side by side. But it changes what is computed: instead of full 300-step episodes from initial state, it computes short-horizon deltas from checkpoints, and tests forgetfulness. The question itself ("does the per-feature effect measured at h rank-match the full 300-step effect?") is about a different measurement (short-horizon effect as a proxy for full effect). This changes what is measured/computed so more compute buys something new (parallel-in-time viability, 6-12x horizon shortening). So "reframe".

But wait — could proposal 2 be "copies" because branches run side by side? The branches are independent and batch massively — that's parallelism. But the reframe aspect: the unit of work changes from full episodes to short segments; the measurement changes (Delta(h) vs Delta(300) rank-match; perturbation divergence). The proposal explicitly says "Change the unit of work". It enables parareal-style speculative rollout — a new kind of computation. More compute buys something it did not before: wall-clock reduction beyond batching (cross-rollout batching was already known via RLinf-VLA). So "reframe".

Hmm, but let me consider: the "kind" definition: "reframe" if it changes what is computed, measured or ordered so that more compute buys something it did not before; "copies" if it only runs the same computation more times, on more items, or side by side.

Proposal 2: The branches compute steered vs unsteered short rollouts — that's still rollouts (same kind of computation), run side by side (parallel). But the key change: evaluating features at short horizons from checkpoints rather than full episodes from scratch, plus perturbation-forgetting tests. This changes what is computed (short-horizon branched segments) and measured (divergence, Delta(h)), and if it works, evaluation becomes fully parallel short segments and parareal becomes viable — wall-clock turns from weeks to hours. That's something more compute (parallel compute) couldn't buy before (since steps within a rollout must run in order). So "reframe".

Actually, there's a subtlety: the problem statement says "Steps within a rollout must run in order, but rollouts are independent: batching hundreds of steered environments ... would run them together". So cross-rollout batching is already known. Proposal 2's contribution beyond that: parallelism in time (within a rollout) via checkpoint branching, and short-horizon proxies. The question asks whether short-horizon effects rank-match full effects — a change in what is measured. So reframe.

But hold on — one might argue proposal 2 is more "copies"-like: branching from checkpoints runs the same rollout computation more times (many branches), side by side. But the branches are from the same base rollout — they're not independent full episodes; they share prefixes. The change is in the unit of work and the measured quantity (short-horizon deltas and divergence). The compute_after says "evaluation becomes fully parallel short segments and parareal-style speculative rollout becomes viable, turning weeks of serial sweep wall-clock into hours". This is a change in what is computed so more compute buys wall-clock reduction it couldn't before. So "reframe".

I'm fairly confident: 1 = reframe, 2 = reframe, 3 = reframe.

Hmm, but maybe one of them is meant to be "copies"? Let me re-read.

Proposal 1: The reframe is measuring per-step proxies within existing rollouts. The measure: "Steer 20 features x 150 rollouts x 300 steps in a ManiSkill-class GPU sim, logging proxies every step". So it runs the same rollouts but logs more. Does more compute buy something new? The claim: "If proxies rank-stabilize at n~10-30, the same budget screens 5-15x more features and tasks per GPU-hour". The change: what is measured (per-step proxies vs binary success), and the ordering criterion (rank by proxy@n rather than success@150). This changes what is measured and ordered so more compute buys more features/tasks coverage. Yes, reframe.

But wait — an alternative reading: proposal 1 still runs the same closed-loop rollouts; it just also logs proxies. The "same budget screens 5-15x more features" — because you need fewer rollouts (n=10-30 instead of 150) to estimate effects via proxies. That is a change in what is measured (proxy effects vs binary success) and how many episodes are needed. It's a reframe of the measurement. I'll stick with reframe.

Actually, hmm, let me think about whether proposal 1 could be "copies". "Copies" = only runs the same computation more times, on more items, or side by side. Proposal 1 does not propose running more of the same; it proposes measuring different things (proxies) within rollouts and using fewer rollouts for screening. That's a measurement change → reframe.

Now the criterion for each:

Criterion: "The question removes the closed-loop dependency: it scores steering effects on fixed, recorded observations (open loop) instead of full closed-loop episodes, and confirms only the top candidates with closed-loop episodes."

Proposal 1: Question: "at what rollout count n does the Spearman correlation between proxy-estimated feature effects and the full 150-rollout success effects exceed 0.9?" — This still runs full closed-loop rollouts (steer 20 features × 150 rollouts × 300 steps). It does not score on fixed recorded observations; it runs closed-loop episodes with per-step logging. So "no". Reason: still closed-loop episodes; proxies logged inside live rollouts, not scored on recorded observations.

Proposal 2: Question: "Do steered and unsteered branches from identical checkpointed states converge or drift apart with horizon h, and does the per-feature effect measured at h in {10,25,50} rank-match the full 300-step effect?" — Branches are short closed-loop segments from checkpointed states; the environment still steps. Not open-loop scoring on recorded observations. So "no". Reason: branches still step the simulator (short closed-loop segments), not open-loop scoring on fixed recorded observations; and confirmation isn't limited to top candidates — it validates rank-match across features.

Hmm, actually the checkpoints are recorded states from base rollouts — but the branches then run closed-loop for h steps. The scoring isn't on fixed recorded observations throughout; only the initial states are recorded. So "no".

Proposal 3: "yes" as discussed. The ranking is pure reanalysis of stored activations/outcomes (fixed, recorded observations), zero new rollouts; only top candidates verified with closed-loop episodes (cloth-sim clamping, 25 rollouts each). Meets criterion.

But wait — is the open-loop scoring of "steering effects"? In proposal 3, the scoring on recorded observations is by activation gap (success minus failure), not by applying steering. Hmm. The criterion says "it scores steering effects on fixed, recorded observations (open loop)". Strictly, scoring steering effects open-loop would mean: take recorded observations, run the steered model forward on them (one forward pass per recorded observation, no environment feedback), and measure the effect (e.g., action difference, activation difference). Proposal 3 doesn't do that; it ranks features by correlational activation gap in recorded logs.

Hmm, this is a judgment call. Let me think about the intent of the criterion. The criterion describes a specific reframe pattern: replace closed-loop evaluation with open-loop scoring on recorded data, then confirm top candidates closed-loop. Proposal 3's pattern: replace causal closed-loop sweeps with correlational mining of recorded logs, then verify top candidates closed-loop. That's essentially the same pattern — the open-loop scoring is the activation-gap ranking on recorded episodes (fixed, recorded observations), and closed-loop episodes confirm only top candidates ("spend rollouts only on verifying top correlational candidates"; "clamp top-5 features, 25 rollouts each").

I think the intended answer is proposal 3 = "yes" for the criterion. The criterion's essence: remove the closed-loop dependency by scoring on recorded data, confirming only top candidates closed-loop. Proposal 3 does that.

Alternatively, one could argue "no" because the open-loop scoring doesn't apply steering per se. But the phrase "scores steering effects" — the activation gap between success and failure episodes is a score of each feature's (hypothesized) steering effect, computed on recorded observations. And the question explicitly compares this to "the published sweep's known causal effects" — i.e., it's scoring (proxy) steering effects on recorded data. And "confirms only the top candidates with closed-loop episodes" — the cloth-sim clamp check on top-5 features. Yes.

Hmm, but one more consideration: the cloth-sim check is 25 rollouts each for top-5 — that's closed-loop confirmation of top candidates. Yes.

Also note: the criterion's open-loop scoring should be on "fixed, recorded observations" — proposal 3 uses "the already-collected 420k rollout logs (plus any recorded cloth episodes)" — fixed, recorded. Yes.

So:
- Index 1: kind=reframe, meets_criterion=no
- Index 2: kind=reframe, meets_criterion=no
- Index 3: kind=reframe, meets_criterion=yes

Wait, should any be "copies" or "other"? Let me reconsider proposal 2's kind once more.

Proposal 2 reframe: "Change the unit of work: run a few long unsteered rollouts with state checkpoints, then branch steered vs unsteered copies from each checkpoint for short horizons; all branches are independent and batch massively, and perturbed unsteered pairs from the same checkpoints directly measure the system's forgetfulness, deciding whether parallel-in-time rollout is even legal."

The question: does the per-feature effect measured at h rank-match the full 300-step effect? This changes what is measured (short-horizon effects from checkpoints) and computed (branched short segments, perturbation tests). More compute (many parallel branches) buys: horizon shortening 6-12x, parareal viability, wall-clock weeks→hours. That's something compute couldn't buy before (steps within a rollout had to be serial). So "reframe".

However, a skeptic might say: branching from checkpoints is just running more rollouts side by side ("copies"). But no — the branches are short segments, and the key measured quantities (Delta(h), perturbation divergence) are new. The compute_after explicitly says wall-clock turns from weeks to hours — a new capability. The change in what is computed: short branched segments instead of full episodes. I'll say "reframe".
